messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Nun
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Sister Margaret Okafor is a 55-year-old Catholic nun of Nigerian-American heritage who has lived and ministered within the same religious community in the rural Midwest for nearly two decades. She came to the attention of a consulting psychologist following a referral from her congregation's spiritual director, who had grown concerned about changes in her demeanor and functioning over the preceding eight months. Margaret presents as composed but visibly strained, choosing her words carefully in a way that suggests long practice at containment rather than ease.

The event that brought Margaret to this point occurred the previous spring, when her younger sister, Adaeze, came to stay at the convent during a period of personal crisis. Margaret had arranged the visit herself, believing the quiet and structure of religious life might offer Adaeze some steadiness. One afternoon, Margaret was leading a prayer group in the chapel when Adaeze, who had been walking alone on the grounds, suffered a massive cardiac event near the small garden at the eastern edge of the property. A novice found her collapsed among the rose beds. By the time Margaret reached her sister, Adaeze was unresponsive. Margaret knelt beside her on the stone path, held her hand, and watched the paramedics work. Adaeze was pronounced dead at the scene.

Margaret remembers certain moments of that afternoon with a precision that feels almost unbearable to her — the particular quality of the afternoon light, the smell of damp soil, the sound of the paramedic's radio crackling. Other moments are simply absent, as though cut from the record entirely. She cannot recall the walk from the chapel to the garden, nor the faces of the sisters who gathered around her afterward. What she does remember arrives without invitation. The sound of a garden gate, the sight of rose bushes through a window, the smell of turned earth during the community's spring planting — any of these can return her instantly and completely to that stone path, kneeling beside Adaeze, the warmth already leaving her sister's hand. This happens in the middle of her daily duties: during the Divine Office, during meals, while instructing the novices she supervises. She has learned to keep her expression still, but those around her have noticed that she sometimes stops mid-sentence and does not finish her thought.

Margaret no longer walks the eastern grounds. She routes her daily movement through the western corridors and yard, and she has quietly arranged for another sister to oversee the garden ministry she once found sustaining. When the community gathered to plant bulbs in autumn — a tradition Margaret had led for years — she remained in her cell, offering an explanation about correspondence that needed attending to. No one pressed her, but the absence was noted. She has also stopped visiting the small memorial that the community placed near the garden in Adaeze's memory, and she cannot bring herself to look at photographs of her sister or attend to the box of Adaeze's belongings that was sent to her from the family home.

What weighs on Margaret most heavily is not grief in the way she would have named it before, but something she experiences as a verdict. She had arranged the visit. She had chosen to be in the chapel rather than with her sister. She had believed, she now tells herself with quiet ferocity, that the convent was safe — and that belief, she is certain, was a form of carelessness. She had failed in the most fundamental duty of a sister, in both the spiritual and the familial sense of that word. She cannot rely on her own judgment, she says, because her judgment is what brought Adaeze to that garden. In the hours before sleep, she performs a private ritual she describes with some embarrassment: a sequence of prayers said in a specific order, a mental rehearsal of protective intentions directed toward each remaining member of her family. She believes, or fears she believes, that if she omits any part of the sequence, something terrible will follow.

Margaret sought help not because the symptoms have worsened, but because she recently found herself unable to pray in any form that felt genuine, and that loss frightened her more than anything else. What she most hopes for, she says quietly, is to be able to trust herself again. What she most fears is that she cannot.
